claim: Many species that run or leap across sparsely vegetated habitats, including horses and deer, evolved the severe reduction or complete loss of foot muscles as skeletal elements elongated and digits were lost.
source: Many species that run or leap across sparsely vegetated habitats, including horses and deer, evolved the severe reduction or complete loss of foot muscles as skeletal elements elongated and digits were lost, and yet the developmental mechanisms remain unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on limb evolution and muscle loss patterns.

claim: The developmental mechanisms of foot muscle loss in species like horses and deer remain unknown.
source: Many species that run or leap across sparsely vegetated habitats, including horses and deer, evolved the severe reduction or complete loss of foot muscles as skeletal elements elongated and digits were lost, and yet the developmental mechanisms remain unknown.
evidence: This is stated explicitly as a knowledge gap in the abstract.

claim: Adult Jaculus jaculus (bipedal jerboa) have no muscles in their feet.
source: Although adults have no muscles in their feet, newborn animals have muscles that rapidly disappear soon after birth.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by anatomical observations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Newborn jerboas have foot muscles that rapidly disappear soon after birth.
source: Although adults have no muscles in their feet, newborn animals have muscles that rapidly disappear soon after birth.
evidence: This is supported by myofiber counts and immunofluorescence data showing muscle presence at P0 and loss by P8.

claim: There is no evidence of apoptotic cell death during stages of peak myofiber loss in jerboa feet.
source: We were surprised to find no evidence of apoptotic or necrotic cell death during stages of peak myofiber loss, countering well-supported assumptions of developmental tissue remodeling.
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assays and cleaved Caspase-3 immunofluorescence showing no apoptotic markers in myofibers.

claim: There is no evidence of necrotic cell death during stages of peak myofiber loss in jerboa feet.
source: We were surprised to find no evidence of apoptotic or necrotic cell death during stages of peak myofiber loss, countering well-supported assumptions of developmental tissue remodeling.
evidence: This is supported by Evans Blue Dye uptake assays and Annexin V staining showing no membrane permeability or phosphatidylserine externalization.

claim: Jerboa foot muscle loss involves hallmarks of muscle atrophy, including ordered disassembly of the sarcomere.
source: We instead see hallmarks of muscle atrophy, including an ordered disassembly of the sarcomere associated with upregulation of the E3 ubiquitin ligases, MuRF1 and Atrogin-1.
evidence: This is supported by multicolor immunofluorescence showing sequential loss of sarcomere proteins and TEM showing progressive sarcomere disorganization.

claim: Jerboa foot muscle loss is associated with upregulation of the E3 ubiquitin ligases MuRF1 and Atrogin-1.
source: We instead see hallmarks of muscle atrophy, including an ordered disassembly of the sarcomere associated with upregulation of the E3 ubiquitin ligases, MuRF1 and Atrogin-1.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data showing significantly elevated expression of MuRF1 and Atrogin-1 in jerboa foot muscle.

claim: The natural loss of muscle in jerboa feet involves cellular mechanisms that are typically associated with disease or injury.
source: We propose that the natural loss of muscle, which remodeled foot anatomy during evolution and development, involves cellular mechanisms that are typically associated with disease or injury.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of atrophy-like mechanisms (sarcomere disassembly, upregulation of atrogenes) in a developmental context.

claim: Muscles in the feet of birds, reptiles, and mammals were lost multiple times in the course of limb evolution.
source: Muscles in the feet of birds, reptiles, and mammals were lost multiple times in the course of limb evolution, usually coinciding with the loss of associated digits and elongation of remaining skeletal elements (Hudson, 1937; Raikow, 1987; Pavaux and Lignereux, 1995; Botelho et al., 2014; Abdala et al., 2015; Berman, 1985; Cunningham, 1883; Souza et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature on limb evolution.

claim: Foot muscle loss in evolution usually coincides with the loss of associated digits and elongation of remaining skeletal elements.
source: Muscles in the feet of birds, reptiles, and mammals were lost multiple times in the course of limb evolution, usually coinciding with the loss of associated digits and elongation of remaining skeletal elements (Hudson, 1937; Raikow, 1987; Pavaux and Lignereux, 1995; Botelho et al., 2014; Abdala et al., 2015; Berman, 1985; Cunningham, 1883; Souza et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to comparative anatomy studies.

claim: The hindlimb architecture of the adult jerboa is strikingly similar by convergence to hooved animals like horses and deer.
source: The hindlimb architecture of the adult jerboa is strikingly similar by convergence to the more familiar hooved animals, like horses and deer, including the disproportionately elongated foot that lacks all intrinsic muscle (Berman, 1985; Cunningham, 1883).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical descriptions and comparative anatomy.

claim: Adult jerboa feet have disproportionately elongated foot that lacks all intrinsic muscle.
source: The hindlimb architecture of the adult jerboa is strikingly similar by convergence to the more familiar hooved animals, like horses and deer, including the disproportionately elongated foot that lacks all intrinsic muscle (Berman, 1985; Cunningham, 1883).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical observations and citations.

claim: Tendons in jerboa feet were retained and expanded in anatomical positions where flexor muscles are absent.
source: The tendons were retained and expanded in each of the anatomical positions where flexor muscles are absent (Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B) and serve to resist hyperextension when the terminal phalanx contacts the ground during locomotion (Lochner et al., 1980; Moore et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical figures and citations to biomechanical studies.

claim: Tendons in jerboa feet serve to resist hyperextension when the terminal phalanx contacts the ground during locomotion.
source: The tendons were retained and expanded in each of the anatomical positions where flexor muscles are absent (Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B) and serve to resist hyperextension when the terminal phalanx contacts the ground during locomotion (Lochner et al., 1980; Moore et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to biomechanical studies.

claim: The evolutionary origin of jerboa intrinsic foot muscle loss lies deep in the phylogenetic tree of Dipodoid rodents.
source: The evolutionary origin of jerboa intrinsic foot muscle loss lies deep in the phylogenetic tree of Dipodoid rodents.
evidence: This is supported by comparative anatomy and phylogenetic data cited in the manuscript.

claim: The number of intrinsic foot muscles are reduced from sixteen to six in pygmy jerboas compared to the ancestral state.
source: Compared to the ancestral state, the number of intrinsic foot muscles are reduced from sixteen to six in pygmy jerboas (Stein, 1990) which diverged from the three-toed jerboa lineage more than 20 million years ago (Wu et al., 2012; Pisano et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies of pygmy jerboas.

claim: Pygmy jerboas diverged from the three-toed jerboa lineage more than 20 million years ago.
source: Compared to the ancestral state, the number of intrinsic foot muscles are reduced from sixteen to six in pygmy jerboas (Stein, 1990) which diverged from the three-toed jerboa lineage more than 20 million years ago (Wu et al., 2012; Pisano et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to phylogenetic studies.

claim: Newborn jerboas have a single m. flexor digitorum brevis and three pinnate m. interossei that are not present in adults.
source: In newborn jerboas, we observed two of the three groups of flexor muscles. While the m. lumbricales never form, the jerboa has a single m. flexor digitorum brevis and three pinnate m. interossei that are not present in adults (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence images of newborn jerboa feet.

claim: The m. lumbricales never form in jerboas.
source: In newborn jerboas, we observed two of the three groups of flexor muscles. While the m. lumbricales never form, the jerboa has a single m. flexor digitorum brevis and three pinnate m. interossei that are not present in adults (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical observations of newborn jerboa feet.

claim: Postnatal growth of vertebrate skeletal muscle typically involves an increase in myofiber number (hyperplasia) within the first week, followed by an increase in myofiber size (hypertrophy).
source: Postnatal growth of vertebrate skeletal muscle typically involves an increase in myofiber number (hyperplasia) within the first week, followed by an increase in myofiber size (hypertrophy) (Chiakulas and Pauly, 1965; Gokhin et al., 2008; White et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on muscle development.

claim: In mice, there is a steady increase in the average number of myofibers in cross section from birth to P8.
source: As expected in the mouse, we observed a steady increase in the average number of myofibers in cross section from birth to P8 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by myofiber counts shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The number of myofibers in the third interosseous of the jerboa foot rapidly declines beginning at approximately P4.
source: In contrast, the number of myofibers in the third interosseous of the jerboa foot rapidly declines beginning at approximately P4, and few myofibers remain by P8 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by myofiber counts shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Few myofibers remain in jerboa foot by P8.
source: In contrast, the number of myofibers in the third interosseous of the jerboa foot rapidly declines beginning at approximately P4, and few myofibers remain by P8 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by myofiber counts shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Multinucleated jerboa foot myofibers are postmitotic.
source: Since multinucleated jerboa foot myofibers are postmitotic (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), we reasoned that BrdU+ nuclei present within Dystroglycan+ myofiber membranes were added by myocyte fusion during the 2-day window after they were labeled as myoblasts or myocytes in S-phase (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by BrdU labeling experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Myocytes fuse to form multinucleated myofibers in jerboa hand muscle at a consistent rate from P0 to P6.
source: When normalized to the total number of myofiber nuclei, we found that myocytes fuse to form multinucleated myofibers in jerboa hand muscle at a consistent rate from P0 to P6.
evidence: This is supported by BrdU fusion assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Myocyte incorporation into jerboa foot muscle decreased significantly after P2.
source: However, their incorporation into jerboa foot muscle decreased significantly after P2 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by BrdU fusion assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Myofiber loss in jerboa feet, which begins at P4, is preceded by reduced myogenesis.
source: These results suggest that myofiber loss, which begins at P4, is preceded by reduced myogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that myocyte fusion decreases before myofiber number declines.

claim: The number of proliferative progenitor cells in jerboa foot muscle significantly decreased from P0 to P4 compared to hand muscles that showed no change over time.
source: Normalized to the total number of myofibers, we found that the number of proliferative progenitor cells in jerboa foot muscle significantly decreased from P0 to P4 compared to hand muscles that showed no change over time (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by short-term BrdU labeling data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A reduced number of muscle progenitor cells might contribute to the reduced prevalence of myocyte fusion events in jerboa feet.
source: These results suggest that a reduced number of muscle progenitor cells might contribute to the reduced prevalence of myocyte fusion events.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that progenitor cell numbers decline before fusion rates decrease.

claim: Jerboa foot muscle cell differentiation and survival in vitro occurs days after cell number begins to decline in vivo.
source: Jerboa foot muscle cell differentiation and survival in vitro days after cell number begins to decline in vivo suggests that loss of jerboa foot myofibers is initiated non-cell autonomously.
evidence: This is supported by primary cell culture experiments showing that jerboa foot muscle cells can differentiate in culture.

claim: Loss of jerboa foot myofibers is initiated non-cell autonomously.
source: Jerboa foot muscle cell differentiation and survival in vitro days after cell number begins to decline in vivo suggests that loss of jerboa foot myofibers is initiated non-cell autonomously.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that jerboa foot muscle cells can differentiate and survive in culture.

claim: TUNEL or cleaved Caspase-3-positive jerboa foot myofibers or cells in their vicinity were an extreme rarity (0.25% of myofibers) in animals ranging from P0 to P8.
source: However, TUNEL or cleaved Caspase-3-positive jerboa foot myofibers or cells in their vicinity were an extreme rarity (0.25% of myofibers) in animals ranging from P0 to P8 and comparable to mouse myofibers suggesting muscle is not eliminated by apoptosis (Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL and cleaved Caspase-3 immunofluorescence data.

claim: The rarity of TUNEL or cleaved Caspase-3-positive jerboa foot myofibers is comparable to mouse myofibers.
source: However, TUNEL or cleaved Caspase-3-positive jerboa foot myofibers or cells in their vicinity were an extreme rarity (0.25% of myofibers) in animals ranging from P0 to P8 and comparable to mouse myofibers suggesting muscle is not eliminated by apoptosis (Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of TUNEL and cleaved Caspase-3 data between mouse and jerboa.

claim: Jerboa foot muscle is not eliminated by apoptosis.
source: However, TUNEL or cleaved Caspase-3-positive jerboa foot myofibers or cells in their vicinity were an extreme rarity (0.25% of myofibers) in animals ranging from P0 to P8 and comparable to mouse myofibers suggesting muscle is not eliminated by apoptosis (Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of apoptotic markers in jerboa foot myofibers.

claim: No EBD fluorescence was observed in jerboa foot myofibers or in surrounding cells.
source: Although we detected EBD in mechanically injured myofibers of the gastrocnemius as a control, we saw no EBD fluorescence in jerboa foot myofibers or in surrounding cells (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by Evans Blue Dye uptake experiments.

claim: No Annexin V immunofluorescence was observed on the surface of jerboa foot myofibers.
source: We also saw no Annexin V immunofluorescence on the surface of jerboa foot myofibers, another hallmark of dying cells that flip Annexin V to the outer plasma membrane (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by Annexin V immunofluorescence data.

claim: No F4/80+ macrophages were found among myofibers from birth to P7 in jerboa feet.
source: However, consistent with the lack of evidence of cell death in the jerboa foot, no F4/80+ macrophages were found among myofibers from birth to P7 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by F4/80 immunofluorescence data.

claim: No evidence of T-cells, B-cells, dendritic cells, natural killer cells, monocytes, or granulocytes was found near jerboa foot myofibers from P4 to P8.
source: Since immune cells other than mature macrophages might be recruited to a site of cell death, we also assessed expression of CD45 and found no evidence of T-cells, B-cells, dendritic cells, natural killer cells, monocytes, or granulocytes near jerboa foot myofibers from P4 to P8 (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by CD45 immunofluorescence data.

claim: Category D and E jerboa foot myofibers have membrane-enclosed vacuoles and large lipid droplets.
source: Additionally, Category D and E cells have membrane-enclosed vacuoles and large lipid droplets (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by TEM images and Oil Red O staining.

claim: Category D and E jerboa foot myofibers do not show swollen cells or organelles, abnormal nuclear morphology, or discontinuous plasma membranes.
source: However, consistent with a lack of evidence for cell death, none of these cells or their organelles appear swollen, nuclear morphology appears normal, plasma membranes seem to be contiguous, and we do not observe an accumulation of autophagic vesicles that typically characterize cell death associated with unregulated autophagy (Mizushima, 2007; Kroemer and Levine, 2008; Denton and Kumar, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by TEM observations and citations to literature on cell death.

claim: No accumulation of autophagic vesicles was observed in degenerating jerboa foot myofibers.
source: However, consistent with a lack of evidence for cell death, none of these cells or their organelles appear swollen, nuclear morphology appears normal, plasma membranes seem to be contiguous, and we do not observe an accumulation of autophagic vesicles that typically characterize cell death associated with unregulated autophagy (Mizushima, 2007; Kroemer and Levine, 2008; Denton and Kumar, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by TEM observations.

claim: Jerboa hand myofibers progressively mature from P0 to P4.
source: Quantification of the percent of myofibers in each category after unblinding revealed the progressive maturation of jerboa hand myofibers and the progressive degeneration of jerboa foot myofibers (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of TEM images shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Jerboa foot myofibers progressively degenerate from P0 to P4.
source: Quantification of the percent of myofibers in each category after unblinding revealed the progressive maturation of jerboa hand myofibers and the progressive degeneration of jerboa foot myofibers (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of TEM images shown in Figure 4G.

claim: There is little difference in the maturation state of hand and foot sarcomeres at birth in jerboas.
source: Compared to later stages, there is little difference in the maturation state of hand and foot sarcomeres at birth.
evidence: This is supported by TEM quantification data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Loss of ultrastructural integrity in jerboa foot myofibers is initiated perinatally, prior to complete myofibril maturation.
source: Loss of ultrastructural integrity is therefore initiated perinatally, prior to complete myofibril maturation in the jerboa foot.
evidence: This is inferred from TEM observations showing early signs of degeneration at P0.

claim: Filamentous aggregates in jerboa feet are enucleate, lack all other recognizable organelles, and are not bounded by a plasma membrane.
source: Our analysis of transmission electron micrographs also revealed the presence of filamentous aggregates that we did not include in our quantifications because they are enucleate, lack all other recognizable organelles, and are not bounded by a plasma membrane.
evidence: This is supported by TEM observations.

claim: Filamentous aggregates in jerboa feet are always closely associated with cells of a fibroblast morphology.
source: Although these aggregates do not appear to be cellular, they are always closely associated with cells of a fibroblast morphology, and most lie between remaining myofibers in a space we presume was also once occupied by a myofiber (Figure 4F,H).
evidence: This is supported by TEM observations.

claim: Filamentous aggregates in jerboa feet contain skeletal muscle myosin heavy chain.
source: To determine if these unusual structures contain muscle protein, we performed immunofluorescence on sections of P4 jerboa foot muscle and found similar aggregates of intensely fluorescent immunoreactivity to skeletal muscle myosin heavy chain.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Cells surrounding filamentous aggregates in jerboa feet express the intracellular pro-peptide of Collagen I.
source: We also found that the surrounding cells, which correlate with the positions of fibroblasts in electron micrographs, express the intracellular pro-peptide of Collagen I (Figure 4I), the major component of tendon and other fibrous connective tissues and of fibrotic tissue after injury (Mann et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Alpha-Actinin, Desmin, Myomesin, Myosin, Titin, and Tropomyosin are each localized to an ordered series of striations in a subset of jerboa foot myofibers.
source: Alpha-Actinin, Desmin, Myomesin, Myosin, Titin, and Tropomyosin are each localized to an ordered series of striations in a subset of myofibers suggesting all are initially incorporated into immature sarcomeres (Figure 5A and Figure 5—source data 1–5).
evidence: This is supported by multicolor immunofluorescence data.

claim: Desmin disorganization is followed together by Myosin and Tropomyosin, then Titin, and lastly Myomesin and α-Actinin during sarcomere disassembly in jerboa feet.
source: Although we could not distinguish such clear categories of mislocalization for each protein relative to all others, we inferred a relative timeline whereby Desmin disorganization is followed together by Myosin and Tropomyosin, then Titin, and lastly Myomesin and α-Actinin (Figure 5B–F and Figure 5—source data 1–5).
evidence: This is inferred from multicolor immunofluorescence observations.

claim: Desmin forms a filamentous network that connects parallel sarcomeres to one another and coordinates myofibril contraction within cells and between neighboring cells.
source: Desmin forms a filamentous network that connects parallel sarcomeres to one another and coordinates myofibril contraction within cells and between neighboring cells (Bär et al., 2004; Capetanaki et al., 2015; Goldfarb et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on Desmin function.

claim: Mutations that cause desminopathies illustrate that Desmin is essential to maintain sarcomere integrity.
source: Mutations that cause desminopathies illustrate that Desmin is essential to maintain sarcomere integrity (Clemen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on desminopathies.

claim: In mouse models of muscle atrophy triggered by fasting or denervation, phosphorylation of Desmin removes the protein from the sarcomere and targets it for ubiquitination and proteolytic degradation prior to degradation of other sarcomere proteins.
source: In mouse models of muscle atrophy triggered by fasting or denervation, phosphorylation of Desmin removes the protein from the sarcomere and targets it for ubiquitination and proteolytic degradation prior to degradation of other sarcomere proteins (Volodin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on Desmin degradation in atrophy.

claim: The observation that Desmin is the first of an ordered sarcomere disassembly in the jerboa foot may reflect targeted degradation of muscle proteins that is similar to muscle atrophy.
source: The observation that Desmin is the first of an ordered sarcomere disassembly in the jerboa foot may reflect targeted degradation of muscle proteins that is similar to muscle atrophy.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of ordered sarcomere disassembly and comparison to atrophy literature.

claim: The ubiquitin-proteasome system is the main pathway through which cellular proteins are degraded during muscle atrophy.
source: The ubiquitin-proteasome system is the main pathway through which cellular proteins are degraded during muscle atrophy, and MuRF1 and Atrogin-1 are E3 ubiquitin ligases among the 'atrogenes' that are highly upregulated (Bodine and Baehr, 2014; Schiaffino et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on muscle atrophy.

claim: MuRF1 and Atrogin-1 are E3 ubiquitin ligases among the 'atrogenes' that are highly upregulated during muscle atrophy.
source: The ubiquitin-proteasome system is the main pathway through which cellular proteins are degraded during muscle atrophy, and MuRF1 and Atrogin-1 are E3 ubiquitin ligases among the 'atrogenes' that are highly upregulated (Bodine and Baehr, 2014; Schiaffino et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on muscle atrophy.

claim: Atrogin-1 expression is 3.1-fold higher in the jerboa foot at P3 compared to expression in the FDS at birth.
source: When normalized to expression in the FDS at birth of each species, Atrogin-1 expression is 3.1-fold higher in the jerboa foot at P3 (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: MuRF1 mRNA expression is significantly elevated at birth in jerboa feet and remains elevated at P3.
source: MuRF1 mRNA expression is already significantly elevated at birth and remains elevated at P3 (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The NF-κB pathway is an upstream mediator of skeletal muscle atrophy.
source: The NF-κB pathway is an upstream mediator of skeletal muscle atrophy (Li et al., 2008) and is both necessary and sufficient to induce MuRF1 expression (Cai et al., 2004; Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on NF-κB and muscle atrophy.

claim: The NF-κB pathway is both necessary and sufficient to induce MuRF1 expression.
source: The NF-κB pathway is an upstream mediator of skeletal muscle atrophy (Li et al., 2008) and is both necessary and sufficient to induce MuRF1 expression (Cai et al., 2004; Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on NF-κB and MuRF1.

claim: NF-κB2 and Relb are each expressed greater than three-fold higher in jerboa foot at birth and at P3.
source: We observed that each gene is expressed greater than three-fold higher in jerboa foot at birth and at P3 (Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5I and 5J.

claim: The progressively disordered ultrastructure of the sarcomere that begins with loss of Desmin localization, the increased expression of multiple genes that are typically upregulated during atrophy, and the lack of evidence for cell death or macrophage infiltration are consistent with observations of atrophying muscle in mice and rats.
source: The progressively disordered ultrastructure of the sarcomere that begins with loss of Desmin localization, the increased expression of multiple genes that are typically upregulated during atrophy, and the lack of evidence for cell death or macrophage infiltration are consistent with observations of atrophying muscle in mice and rats (Volodin et al., 2017; Bonaldo and Sandri, 2013; Sakuma et al., 2015; von Haehling et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to literature on muscle atrophy in rodents.

claim: Myofiber loss in the jerboa foot does not seem to be simply explained by an atrophic response to denervation.
source: Despite the similarities to muscle atrophy, myofiber loss in the jerboa foot does not seem to be simply explained by an atrophic response to denervation.
evidence: This is inferred from observations that differ from typical denervation atrophy.

claim: Chronic denervation in mice (100 days after nerve transection at P14) reduced the size but not the number of individual myofibers.
source: First, and in contrast to the rapid rate of jerboa foot myofiber loss, chronic denervation in mice (100 days after nerve transection at P14) reduced the size but not the number of individual myofibers (Moschella and Ontell, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on denervation in mice.

claim: The post-synaptic Acetylcholine Receptor (AchR) exclusively coincides with the presynaptic neuronal protein, Synaptophysin, in neonatal jerboa foot muscles.
source: Additionally, we found that the post-synaptic Acetylcholine Receptor (AchR) exclusively coincides with the presynaptic neuronal protein, Synaptophysin, in neonatal jerboa foot muscles (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the mouse, AchR clusters are present in a broad domain of fetal muscle prior to innervation and are refined to nerve terminals in response to chemical synapse activity before birth.
source: In the mouse, AchR clusters are present in a broad domain of fetal muscle prior to innervation and are refined to nerve terminals in response to chemical synapse activity before birth (Yang et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on AchR clustering in mice.

claim: The refinement of AchR clusters in jerboa foot muscles suggests that the muscles are not only innervated at birth but are also responsive to motor inputs.
source: The refinement of AchR clusters in jerboa foot muscles suggests that the muscles are not only innervated at birth but are also responsive to motor inputs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of refined AchR clusters in jerboa foot muscles.

claim: There are remarkable similarities in the histology of jerboa and horse foot muscle compared to human clinical observations of tissue remodeling that follows rotator cuff tear characterized by muscle atrophy, myofiber loss, and fibrosis.
source: Indeed, there are remarkable similarities in the histology of jerboa and horse foot muscle compared to human clinical observations of tissue remodeling that follows rotator cuff tear characterized by muscle atrophy, myofiber loss, and fibrosis (Souza et al., 2010; Gibbons et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies on rotator cuff pathology.

claim: Foot muscle atrophy in the jerboa may be one of many cellular responses associated with injury or disease in humans that is utilized in the normal development and physiology of other species.
source: Foot muscle atrophy in the jerboa may be one of many cellular responses associated with injury or disease in humans that is utilized in the normal development and physiology of other species.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: There is less of a clear divide between natural and pathological states than typically thought.
source: These data suggest that there is less of a clear divide between natural and pathological states than typically thought.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Studies of non-traditional species may reveal the mechanisms of evolutionary malleability and advance our understanding of fundamental biological processes that are typically associated with pathological conditions.
source: Studies of non-traditional species may not only reveal the mechanisms of evolutionary malleability, but may also advance our understanding of fundamental biological processes that are typically associated with pathological conditions.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader implications of the study.

claim: Limb muscle progenitors are specified from mesodermal cells at the ventrolateral edge of the dermomyotome in somites aligned with the prospective limb.
source: Briefly, limb muscle progenitors are specified from mesodermal cells at the ventrolateral edge of the dermomyotome in somites aligned with the prospective limb.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on limb muscle development.

claim: Limb muscle progenitor cells delaminate and migrate into the limb bud as dorsal and ventral muscle masses that proliferate and initiate a myoblast specification program.
source: These cells delaminate and migrate into the limb bud as dorsal and ventral muscle masses that proliferate and initiate a myoblast specification program (Chevallier et al., 1977; Christ et al., 1977; Hayashi and Ozawa, 1991; Murphy and Kardon, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on limb muscle development.

claim: The muscle masses are subdivided into individual muscle groups in response to cues from the developing muscle connective tissue, which is derived from limb field lateral plate mesoderm.
source: The muscle masses are then subdivided into individual muscle groups in response to cues from the developing muscle connective tissue, which is derived from limb field lateral plate mesoderm (Hayashi and Ozawa, 1991; Kardon, 1998; Kardon et al., 2003; Wortham, 1948).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on limb muscle development.

claim: Muscle masses initiate a differentiation program, which includes cell fusion to form aligned multinucleated myofibers.
source: They then initiate a differentiation program, which includes cell fusion to form aligned multinucleated myofibers (Abmayr and Pavlath, 2012; Kelly and Zacks, 1969).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on muscle differentiation.

claim: Each differentiated myofiber produces an assemblage of Z-body proteins, Actin filaments, and non-muscle Myosin that form premyofibrils.
source: Each differentiated myofiber produces an assemblage of Z-body proteins, Actin filaments, and non-muscle Myosin that form premyofibrils (Ono, 2010; Rhee et al., 1994; Sanger and Sanger, 2008; Sanger et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on myofibril assembly.

claim: Desmin, α-Actinin, and the Z-body portion of Titin begin to organize during myofibril assembly.
source: Desmin, α-Actinin, and the Z-body portion of Titin also begin to organize (Furst et al., 1989; Sanger et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on myofibril assembly.

claim: Subsequent uncoiling of Titin increases Z-body spacing, and integration of embryonic skeletal muscle Myosin results in formation of nascent myofibrils.
source: Subsequent uncoiling of Titin increases Z-body spacing, and integration of embryonic skeletal muscle Myosin results in formation of nascent myofibrils (Ono, 2010; Sanger et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on myofibril assembly.

claim: Hindlimb denervation or immobilization in adult jerboas causes gradual loss of muscle mass, primarily through a significant reduction in the diameter of individual myofibers.
source: However, the rapid and complete loss of myofibers in the neonatal jerboa foot does not appear to simply reflect a species-level difference in the animal's generalized response to disuse atrophy, since hindlimb denervation or immobilization in adult jerboas causes gradual loss of muscle mass, primarily through a significant reduction in the diameter of individual myofibers (AlWohaib and Alnaqeeb, 1997; Aryan and Alnaqeeb, 2002).
